The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo

Diageo (DGE-GB): a high floor under earnings at a trough multiple, but the upside rests on a sector re-rating and on US share holding

26 November 2026, for Richard

Money is in US dollars and fiscal years end 30 June (FY2027 is the year to June 2027). EPS is on the brokers' basis unless marked "model". Probabilities are my judgements. Conventions, data dates and the one input I changed are in the end notes.

#0 Summary: key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in three sentences. Diageo, the world's leading spirits franchise, is one year into a repair under a new chief executive, and its shares trade at the 2nd percentile of their own ten-year valuation range. Diageo's earnings for the next 18 months are unusually well bounded, because two drivers that management controls and has dated set them: overhead savings and debt repayment. Diageo's share price is not well bounded, because it will be set mostly by a multiple that belongs to the whole spirits industry, and that multiple turns on whether US spirits stop shrinking.
$1.68 / 1.77 / 1.86My EPS for FY2027-29, within 1% of consensus: a high floor and a low ceiling.
13.8xTwo-year forward P/E, at the 2nd percentile of its ten-year range. Trough 11x; my fair range 16-17.5x.
+19%My probability-weighted return to December 2027, against the model's +73% at the guideline 21.6x.
~60%Chance that guidance is not cut at any of the next six reporting events.

What matters most.

  1. Diageo's earnings have a high floor. I expect EPS of about $1.68, $1.77 and $1.86 for FY2027-29, growth of 2%, 5% and 5%. By FY2028 the two controllable drivers (savings and lower finance charges) add about 18c, and two subtractions that are already known (the sale of East African Breweries and the roll-off of currency hedge gains) take back about 10c. Trading therefore has to contribute almost nothing. I put the chance of FY2027 EPS landing within 3% of $1.68 at about 75%.
  2. Diageo's earnings also have a low ceiling, and consensus already sits at that ceiling. My EPS forecasts are within 1% of consensus and contain no upgrade cycle. What the case offers instead is the end of a 36-month downgrade cycle: about a 60% chance that guidance is not cut at any of the next six reporting events. After three years of cuts, an end to downgrades is worth having, but it is a different claim from "upgrades ahead".
  1. On Richard's test of unusually positive skew, Diageo's valuation passes and its earnings revisions do not yet. The multiple is nearer its floor (11 times, touched in March 2026) than its ceiling. But FY2027 guidance holds cushions only in cash and gross savings, none in profit, and my EPS forecast is the market's EPS forecast. The case becomes the kind Richard looks for only if US market share holds (point 6).
4. The likeliest disappointment is a result whose total is met and whose composition misses. Management can protect profit by keeping more of the savings. The bad outcome to expect, with a 20-25% probability, is EPS delivered while North American sales, market share or gross margin miss. The market would read that result as evidence of a weaker franchise, and the market would be right.
5. The return depends on the multiple far more than on earnings. At an unchanged 13.8 times, earnings growth and dividends give about 7% a year. Viewforth's guideline multiple of 21.6 times gives the model's +73% to December 2027. My central range of 16 to 17.5 times gives roughly +20-35%, and my probability-weighted return is about +19%. A fall back to the 11-times trough costs about 15%.
6. One development would change the character of the case: Diageo's US market share holding. US share holding is the only event that would raise earnings, remove the doubt about franchise quality and open the upper half of the multiple range at the same time. The company dates US share stabilisation to FY2028. Evidence of it before FY2028 is the positive surprise to watch for, month by month.
7. August 2027 is the pivotal date, and its outcome is two-sided. The FY2027 results in August 2027 bring FY2028 guidance from a new finance director and the first buyback decision. Diageo's own leverage target limits that first buyback to about $0.5-1.0bn, against the $2bn a year the optimists describe.

The five judgements that move the value most (worked through in #9): the multiple the market pays for spirits; how much of the $1bn of savings survives reinvestment; North American sales; cash, debt and the size of the buyback; and US trade policy.

Where I differ from the market.

Against the optimists (Jefferies, Bernstein)

I see no beat-and-raise cycle in profit, and I expect a smaller first buyback.

Against the pessimists (Morgan Stanley)

I expect guidance to be met and the earnings floor to hold.

Against the model's return of record

A multiple of 21.6 times is where the bull case ends, not where the central case sits.

#1 The operating environment: a moderate headwind that has stopped worsening

Conclusion: the operating environment is a moderate net headwind that has stopped worsening, with narrow tailwinds and broad headwinds, so the environment will not carry the case.

Evidence.

  • The largest profit pool is still shrinking. North America earns 40-45% of group profit. In October, Diageo's US retail sales were falling about 6% in a flat market. Diageo is losing share in categories that cover 65% of its North American portfolio, and it has cut shelf prices on about 70% of its US product lines. Part of the decline is structural: 54% of US adults now drink, the lowest share in Gallup's 90 years of polling. Part is cyclical: middle-income budgets are squeezed, and distributors pay 7-9% to finance their stock.
  • Oversupply keeps prices down. Agave costs about a sixth of its peak price, American whiskey stocks have tripled since 2012, and cognac houses hold about ten years of sales in cask. Aged stock cannot leave the market, so these gluts will depress prices for years.
  • The growth pockets are real but small. India, Guinness, canned cocktails, alcohol-free beer, Latin America and travel retail together add 2 to 2.5 points to group organic growth. US spirits subtract 1 to 2 points.
  • The rate of change has improved. US distributor destocking has ended, the US tariff on Scotch was removed in April 2026, the fear about weight-loss drugs has shrunk to a one-off effect of about 2% on volume, and comparisons in China are easy.
  • Policy and the macro backdrop are mixed. India's trade deal with the UK halves India's tariff on Scotch, while Indian customs is holding bulk Scotch at the ports; either way, India is only about 4% of profit. US trade policy is the larger issue and is assessed in #9. A US ten-year yield near 5% holds down the multiples investors pay for consumer staples.

Headwinds: broad

A shrinking US profit pool; share losses and price cuts across most of the US portfolio; agave, American whiskey and cognac gluts; a US ten-year yield near 5%.

Tailwinds: narrow

Six growth pockets; destocking over; the Scotch tariff removed; the weight-loss drug fear reduced to a one-off; easy Chinese comparisons.

Inference. The operating environment has stopped getting worse, but it is not yet helping. Because the growth pockets and the US drag roughly cancel, "broadly flat" is the right external baseline for FY2027, with low single-digit growth after that. No market-led recovery belongs in the forecasts before FY2028.

So what. Diageo is a self-help case, and any external improvement is free optionality. That optionality is concentrated in one place: every external pressure (price cuts, tariffs, the mix shift to canned cocktails, lost share) lands on the same North American gross margin.

Strongest counter-case. The US weakness may be more cyclical than I allow. At the November annual general meeting, management itself pointed to living costs. After the FY2015 destock, Diageo's organic growth recovered from a small decline to 5% within three years. If US spirits return to 2-3% value growth, group growth of 3-4% is within reach and the forecasts are too low.

What would change my view. For the better: two consecutive quarters of US category value growth, with Diageo's share loss under half a point. For the worse: Pernod Ricard or Bacardi matching Diageo's price cuts in tequila and whisky after the holiday season.

Against the market. I agree with consensus on the direction of the environment. I am slightly lower on FY2029 organic growth (2.2%, against the company's 2.5% target), because the company's figure needs share gains rather than market growth.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. The external balance is a moderate net headwind that has stopped worsening: the US profit pool (40-45% of profit) faces a structural fall in drinking, aged-stock and agave gluts that hold prices down for years and a guided $70m of net tariffs, while India, Guinness, travel retail and easy China comparisons add 2-2.5 points and destocking has ended; consensus sales growth of 0.6% (7.7th percentile) is honest for the business after the EABL sale. I sit a little above the group's 29 because the US category is flat rather than falling and the rate of change has improved (Diageo's own US share loss is scored in topic 2), so it lies between Entra's mildly negative rates backdrop and Vodafone's below-typical mature market.

#2 Corporate change forces: strong on cost and capital, unproven on market share

Conclusion: Diageo's internal change is strong, broad and well funded on cost and capital, and unproven where it must turn cost savings into market share.

Evidence.

  • Who. Sir Dave Lewis became chief executive on 1 January 2026 and had a new operating model live within seven months. The heads of North America and Asia Pacific are new, and the Chair dates from February 2025. A new finance director, Joanne Wilson, arrives in 2027.
  • What. The strategy moves from premium brands only to the full price ladder, from transactional selling to planning categories with retailers, and from 84% on-time delivery towards 98%. It is funded by $1.2bn of restructuring that releases $1bn of savings: $850m of overheads (40% delivered in FY2027, 55% in FY2028) and $150m in the supply chain.
  • Balance sheet. The dividend was halved, saving about $1bn a year. East African Breweries (EABL) is being sold for $2.3bn, at 17 times EBITDA, and United Spirits' cricket team for about $1.9bn, at 84 times.
  • Incentives. Long-term executive pay now rests on free cash flow, EPS and return on capital.
  • The costs of change. Advertising and promotion spending fell 13% organically in FY2026. That cut, about $480m, was four times the year's organic profit growth. Staff turnover has risen to 20%. The finance director who built the plan is leaving mid-plan. The chief executive does not yet own shares.

Inference. Diageo has the strongest internal change forces among European spirits houses, and they are weighted towards cost, capital and organisation. The commercial changes are the right ones, and they are unproven.

The insight that organises the rest of the memo: gross margin is where reinvestment will show.

Management makes three promises: to reinvest the savings in competitiveness, to hold advertising at about 16% of sales, and still to grow profit at a mid-single-digit rate. All three promises can hold together only if the reinvestment is made in prices and trade terms. The reinvestment will therefore appear as weaker price/mix and gross margin, not as a cost line. Gross margin is the line that reveals reinvestment, and the advertising ratio is the check on whether management is being straight about it.

So what. Give high weight to Diageo's cost, cash and leverage commitments and low weight to its market-share path. Read rising margins combined with falling advertising as a warning, not a win.

Strongest counter-case. Diageo's repair may be a "false friend" turnaround, in which margins improve while the franchise erodes. In Deutsche Bank's study, drinks companies that cut brand spending lost a cumulative 483 basis points of gross margin and did not regain share. Campari, the company gaining US share, is doing the opposite of cutting brand spending.

What would change my view. For the better: a half-year result with overheads down by more than 100 basis points of sales and advertising at or above 16% of sales. For the worse: profit growth delivered by cutting advertising again, slippage in the phasing of savings, or departures of senior commercial staff.

Against the market. Every broker accepts the cost savings; the debate is how much of the savings Diageo keeps in profit. My 40% sits between Jefferies' 30% and the company's own algorithm, which implies about half.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. A clear, funded, multi-part reset under a proven turnaround chief executive (new operating model in seven months, $1bn of savings worth about 12c of EPS by FY2028, $4.2bn of disposals, the dividend halved, pay tied to cash, EPS and returns) will lift earnings within three years, but it is a repair weighted to cost and capital, its commercial leg is unproven, and it carries its own problems: advertising cut 13%, 20% staff turnover, a finance director leaving mid-plan. That puts it just below the group's 72, above OEM's acquisition push and below Theon's growth pivot.

#3 Value chain, competitive advantage, financial profile and management: a wide moat with one damaged section

Conclusion: Diageo has a favourable industry and a wide moat with one damaged section (US demand), an above-average financial profile weakened by mediocre cash conversion and high debt, and a dynamic management whose culture and commercial record are still to be earned.

Evidence, area by area.

Inference. Diageo's supply-side advantages (time, scale and regulation) are intact. Its demand-side advantage in the US was shallower than a decade of premium pricing suggested. Its execution advantage decayed, and execution is the most repairable of the three.

So what. The business is better than a 2nd-percentile multiple implies and less good than its ten-year median multiple implies. That gap frames the fair-multiple judgement in #11.

Strongest counter-case. Scale did not stop Diageo losing US share. Profit may be moving permanently to distributors and retailers. If brown spirits decline structurally, maturing stock turns from an asset into a write-down. And Lewis's Tesco toolkit suits the 70% of sales made through retailers, not brand building.

What would change my view. Guinness losing more of the British stout market than the 5% Murphy's has already taken; a further fall in return on capital; or any impairment of maturing stock.

Against the market. Sell-side opinion is split between "great franchise, fixable" and "structurally lower growth". I sit between the two: the franchise is fixable, and its normal growth rate is lower than its history.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. The supply-side moat is first-rate (21% of international spirits against 6% for the number two, over half of aged Scotch, US franchise law, private label under 1%), but the US demand moat proved shallow (share down from 17.2% to 15.1%, price cuts on 70% of lines), returns on recent capital are poor (ROIC 16.3% to 13.4%, 5.5% reported at the 41st percentile after impairments, buybacks at 20-25 times), leverage is 3.1 times, conversion 77%, and management is decisive but unproven in spirits. The 81st-percentile operating margin is real; I sit above the groups (45-57) for the global franchise and just below Carlsberg, whose position is comparably strong with better current delivery, and above Helios Towers.

#4 Guidance: realistic on profit, conservative on cash, with one good year of record

Conclusion: Diageo's guidance is realistic rather than conservative on profit, conservative on cash and gross savings, and backed by one good year after several poor ones.

Evidence.

  • FY2027 profit guidance has no hidden cushion. FY2027 guidance is flat organic sales, low-to-mid-single-digit organic profit growth, about $2bn of free cash flow after about $850m of restructuring cash, and leverage of about 2.75 times. The profit range equals $115-285m of growth. Adding about $70m of net tariffs, the range needs $185-355m out of roughly $380m of gross savings, before any price investment or cost inflation.
  • The cushions are in cash, gross savings and India. FY2026 free cash flow was $3.21bn, against a $3bn floor. The previous savings programme delivered $540m, against $300m guided. India is guided to grow 4-6%, against Jefferies' 10%. The three-year cash target of about $8bn compares with my $8.8bn.
  • Proactivity is low. First-quarter sales beat consensus (+1.4% against (0.4)%), and management simply repeated guidance. The three-year cash target was set below the $10bn the market expected. The chief executive called the quarter "a small step".
  • The record is short and good, and the longer record is poor. Over twelve months, FY2026 profit, EPS and cash all came in ahead of a lowered bar. Over three to five years, Diageo issued a profit warning in November 2023, abandoned a 5-7% growth target, and cut guidance and the dividend in February 2026.

Inference. Management is building a habit of promising little on sales and over-delivering on cost and cash. That habit has one year of evidence behind it. Guidance is therefore a floor, not a springboard.

So what. Expect guidance to be met and repeated. A raise, if one comes, will be in cash or the savings total, not in profit.

Strongest counter-case. Guidance may be less safe than it looks. The FY2027 margin gain is weighted to the second half. One of the two second-half quarters has an easy comparison and the other a hard one, because the prior year included stocking ahead of the football World Cup. A new finance director also has every reason to set FY2028 guidance low: I put the chance of a cautious first FY2028 guide at 35%.

What would change my view. A raise in cash or savings guidance on 10 February 2027 would be the first hard evidence of deliberate conservatism. A trim to the profit range would break the pattern.

Against the market. Jefferies suspects management of low-balling guidance to rebuild a habit of beats. I agree for cost and cash, and disagree for profit.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. Since the February 2026 rebasing the new team has met or beaten every floor (FY2026 profit, EPS and $3.21bn of cash ahead of a lowered bar, a first-quarter sales beat, the last savings programme at $540m against $300m), and current guidance is conservative on cash and gross savings but only realistic on profit; against that, the two-to-three-year record holds a profit warning in November 2023, an abandoned 5-7% growth target and a guidance and dividend cut, which the brief weighs heavily. That places it below the groups (55, 47), just above Instalco's beat after a year of missed targets and below Sdiptech's untested new targets.

#5 Pricing power, leverage, cost-out and feedback loops: three years of profit growth from cost and financing

Conclusion: Diageo's levers produce outsized profit growth for three years through cost and financing, not through pricing or revenue, and the supply of both cost savings and debt reduction runs out around FY2029.

Evidence, lever by lever.

LeverState todayContribution to FY2029
Pricing powerNegative in North America; latent in Guinness, Indian premium spirits and luxury ScotchPrice/mix of (0.3)%, +0.5% and +1.0% in FY2027-29, half the old 2-3%
Operating leverageEach sales dollar contributes about 43.5c after cost of goods and advertising, against a 29% operating marginOne point of organic sales moves operating profit about 1.5%, and more on the way down, because the volume being lost is the most profitable
Cost-outOverheads at about 14.6% of salesOverheads fall to about 11.8% of sales (company target 10.5%): the largest lever
Financial leverageNet finance charges of $816m in FY2026, 14% of operating profitAbout $640m by FY2029, as net debt falls from $20bn to $14bn
Feedback loopsOne positive financial loop and one negative commercial loop in North America (shown below)The financial loop compounds with high confidence; the commercial loop is slowing, not reversed

Inference. Diageo's profit will grow faster than its revenue for three years: EPS up 5-6% a year on organic sales up 1-2%. But the mechanism is cost removal and debt repayment, not revenue growth pulling profit up behind it, and both cost removal and debt repayment are finite. By FY2029 the savings are spent, and rising depreciation takes 15-20 basis points off the margin each year.

So what. The model is right to flatten the operating margin at about 31.5% after FY2029, because from then on growth needs revenue. The constructive point is that operating leverage is symmetric: if North America stabilises, each point of sales adds 1.5% to operating profit and also reduces the need to reinvest, so the two largest EPS sensitivities (savings kept and North American sales) improve together.

Strongest counter-case. Morgan Stanley argues that margins fall once the savings end, and that the drop-through from falling sales, excluding savings, has been 85%. If the commercial loop has not turned by FY2029, the savings will have been spent on defending share.

What would change my view. A stable gross margin with rising North American volume would show the commercial loop reversing. A gross margin down more than 100 basis points with volume still falling would show the loop tightening.

Against the market. Consensus has operating margins of 31.8% and 32.3% for FY2029 and FY2030, while the model has 31.4% and 31.6%. I think consensus is too high for those years.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. Structurally the operating gearing is ordinary (about 43.5c contribution per sales dollar against a 29% margin, so one point of sales moves profit about 1.5%, more on the way down) and pricing power is negative in North America and only latent elsewhere, while cost-out scope is large (overheads from 14.6% towards 11.8% of sales) and financial leverage works for EPS as net debt falls from $20bn to $14bn. EPS growing 5-6% on 1-2% organic sales is mostly finite cost and interest removal with a negative commercial loop, so it sits just above the typical mix, coherent with Economic strength 45 and Financial forecasts 35 lifted by the cost-out lever.

#6 Forecast financials: mid-single-digit EPS growth built on savings and lower interest

Conclusion: Diageo's forecasts show mid-single-digit EPS growth with rising margins and cash, better than the last four years and worse than the franchise's history, with double-digit growth only in the bull tail.

Four notes on reading the forecast table.

  1. Reported revenue falls for two years only because EABL (about $1.1bn of sales) leaves the group.
  2. The model's 4% fall in FY2027 EPS is largely an artefact of the tax charge the model's convention uses for FY2026; on the brokers' basis, EPS rises 2%.
  3. The model's own FY2027 free cash flow ($3.2bn) omits restructuring cash, so the table shows my cross-check of $2.2bn.
  4. My cross-check EPS row includes my lower finance charges; the model's rows do not yet.
Is there double-digit growth? Not in the base case. EPS compounds at about 5.5% a year from FY2027 to FY2031, and with a 2% dividend yield the business offers about 7% a year before any change in the multiple. Double-digit growth needs three things together: half the savings kept, buybacks of $2bn a year, and North America growing. That combination is the bull tail (Bernstein's 11% a year), not the centre.
Is the outlook better than the past? Yes against the last four years, no against the decade before. EPS fell 4.9% a year from FY2022 to FY2026; in the forecasts the margin regains its FY2023 peak by FY2029, and free cash flow of $3.2-3.9bn compares with an average of $2.85bn over FY2024-26. But organic growth of about 2% is half the 40-year norm, and EPS does not pass its FY2022 level until FY2031.

What the EPS growth is made of (FY2026 to FY2028, in cents of EPS). The forecast barely needs the market. Two controllable drivers add about 17.6c: savings kept in profit (+12.3c, on $360m) and lower finance charges (+5.3c). Two known subtractions take away 10.3c: disposals ((7.7)c) and the roll-off of currency hedge gains ((2.6)c). Everything else (trading, the Moët Hennessy associate, minorities and tax) nets to about +4c.

The finance-charge input I changed shows there is no hidden upside below the operating line. The earlier Analyst corrected finance charges using an estimated FY2026 base of about $850m. The annual report has since given the actual figures: net finance charges of $816m, of which other finance charges were only $4m, against the $50m a year the earlier Analyst carried forward. With those figures, associates' profit of $218m and minorities of $221m, FY2026 EPS reconciles to within half a cent of the reported 165.3c, on a tax rate of 24.3% applied before associates. The reconciliation also supports the model's reading of the tax guidance. I have therefore set finance charges at $765m, $660m, $635m, $635m and $655m for FY2027-31, about $45m a year lower, which adds about 1.5c to EPS in each year and changes no conclusion. The practical message is that the "hidden upside below the operating line" that earlier work hoped for is mostly not there: on the corrected figures, our FY2027 pre-tax profit sits on consensus.

Strongest counter-case. My EPS matches consensus partly for different reasons: lower revenue and operating profit from FY2028, offset by lower finance charges and buybacks. A forecast built that way is exposed to how results are composed.

What would change my view. On 10 February 2027, the half-year finance charge (I expect about $400m), the tax charge and the profit attributed to minorities will confirm or correct the EPS bridge.

Against the market. My EPS is in line with consensus for FY2027-28 and 1-2% below it for FY2029-30; my operating profit is 2-4% below consensus from FY2028.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. Growth of nil to 5% gives D, placed at the top of the band because the measure sits on the 5% line, the FY2027 figure is held down by the EABL sale and the hedge roll-off, and the margin rises from 29.0% to about 31.5%, regaining its FY2023 peak; it goes no higher because the growth is cost removal and lower interest on organic sales of about 2%, not revenue, and the margin flattens once the savings are spent.

#7 Scope for upgrades over 6-12 months: little in profit, some in cash and capital returns

Conclusion: there is little scope for profit upgrades in the next 6-12 months, some scope in cash and capital returns, and a real but unspectacular improvement ahead in the narrative.

Evidence: my probabilities.

RaisedHeldCut
FY2027 guidance, at the half-year results on 10 February 202710%75%15%
FY2027 consensus EPS, over the next three events20%55%25%
FY2028 consensus EPS, over the next three events20%50%30%
FY2029-30 consensus operating profit, over 18 months10%25%65%, by 3-4%

Shading darkens with probability; red marks the one likely cut.

  • Upgrades can come from six places, mostly below operating profit. First, cash: I have $2.2bn of FY2027 free cash flow, against $2bn guided. Second, the savings total: there is a 30% chance it is raised within 18 months, as the last programme's total was. Third, a first buyback, which is absent from published estimates; each $1bn of buyback adds about 0.8% to EPS after the interest forgone. Fourth, Moët Hennessy, which brokers model cautiously while LVMH's wines and spirits margin recovers. Fifth, a sale of the Chinese spirits business, which would bring cash for buybacks and slightly dilute EPS. Sixth, a refund of the US tariffs struck down in February 2026: Campari and Rémy Cointreau have collected their refunds, Diageo has not mentioned one, and a refund would arrive through cost of goods with a lag of about two quarters.
  • Cuts will come first from a mechanical source. Several large brokers still include EABL, and when the EABL sale completes they will cut revenue by about 5% and operating profit by about 3.5%. Cuts will then come from outer-year margins (#5) and from depreciation, which consensus holds flat while capital spending runs far above depreciation.
  • The narrative can improve in three dated steps. The narrative can move from "broken premium model, stretched balance sheet" to "cost-led stabilisation with cash coming back" as savings reach profit (February 2027), leverage reaches about 2.75 times, and the first buyback is announced (August 2027). The step after that, to "share-gaining compounder", needs evidence from the US.

Inference. The scope for upgrades over 6-12 months is small, lies mostly below operating profit, and is partly conditional. The asymmetric feature of the case is the low probability of cuts.

So what, practically: do not mistake the EABL adjustment for the thesis failing. The dashboard's sell-side momentum reading will probably weaken around the EABL completion, because revisions to sales and EBITDA will turn negative mechanically, for reasons that carry no information about trading. Read the EPS line and the reasons behind its revisions instead.

Strongest counter-case. The savings are front-loaded (40% of overhead savings fall in FY2027), so they could land faster than management's "back-half weighted" messaging implies, and the previous programme's 80% over-delivery suggests that Diageo habitually guides low on cost. A clean first half with overheads sharply lower would push FY2027 EPS towards $1.72 and restart upgrades.

What would change my view. Half-year organic profit growth above 3% without a lower advertising ratio.

Against the market. The constructive brokers expect a habit of beating; Bernstein has FY2027 EPS near $1.82. I do not expect a habit of beating. The cautious brokers expect margins to disappoint within the year. I do not expect that either.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is more likely held (75%) than raised (10%), with a slightly larger chance of a cut (15%); consensus EPS is skewed a little down for FY2027 (20% up, 25% down) and FY2028 (20/30), outer-year operating profit is 65% likely to be cut by 3-4%, and the EABL completion will cut revenue and profit mechanically, so with organic growth near 1% even small cuts score large on Richard's rule. The upsides are small and below operating profit (an unmodelled first buyback worth about 0.4-0.8% of EPS, cash, the savings total) and the narrative should improve modestly, coherent with the group's 44, between Tele2's limited further raises and IMCD's recovery-dependent scope.

#8 Current momentum: positive and early, but led by the sector

Conclusion: Diageo's momentum is moderately positive and early across estimates, narrative and price, with no guidance upgrades, and the sector is leading it more than the company is.

Evidence (dashboard, 20-23 November 2026).

  • Guidance. There have been no upgrades. Management repeated guidance after a first-quarter sales beat, and beat its cost and cash targets in FY2026.
  • Estimates. FY2027 EPS revisions are +1%, +2% and +4% over one, three and six months, and (3)% over twelve. Sales revisions are 0%, 0% and (1)%, so the profit upgrades are cost-led. Target prices are up 7-9%. Buy ratings make up 46% of ratings, up six points in six months. Sell-side momentum is rated B, with the second-best revision score in the beverage sector.
  • Price. Technical momentum is rated B. The shares are 16.6% above their 200-day average and 3.5% below their 52-week high, up 16.3% in six months and 6.4% in twelve, with relative strength at the 64th percentile. The 200-day average has risen in only two of the last twelve months, the signature of an early uptrend.
  • Narrative. Press and broker opinion has moved from capitulation to cautious approval of the new chief executive.
  • Peers. Diageo's momentum grades are among the best in its peer group, while Pernod Ricard's are the weakest.

Inference. Diageo's momentum is positive, early and largely borrowed from the sector. Over six months the share price rose about four times as fast as estimates, so the multiple did most of the work, moving from about 12 to about 14 times. About three-quarters of that price gain was common to beverage peers. Pernod Ricard, Diageo's closest twin, has the weakest momentum in the group, which shows that the spirits industry has not turned even though Diageo has.

So what. Momentum supports the case without yet confirming it. The market has barely given Diageo company-specific credit for its plan. That credit is still to be earned, and the sector-driven gain so far can be withdrawn for reasons unrelated to Diageo.

Strongest counter-case. I may be underrating Diageo's momentum. EPS revisions have turned positive after a three-year downgrade cycle, the earnings momentum rating is the joint best in the sector, and the price is near its high: early uptrends look exactly like this.

What would change my view. For the better: the 200-day average rising for four or more consecutive months, and EPS revisions staying positive through the EABL adjustment. For the worse: a sector reversal. Deutsche Bank calls the sector's 2026 rally "more froth than fizz", and Deutsche Bank's own work warns that leveraged defensive stocks de-rate first.

Against the market. I share the market's caution on the sector's rally, but I do not apply it in full to Diageo, whose multiple is still at the bottom of its own history and below the sector's.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. One measure negative and one positive gives C; I place it in the upper part of the band because the parts lean positive (three-month EPS revisions +5% at the 79.5th percentile, many times the revenue growth rate, target prices up 7-9%, buy ratings up six points, the narrative improved, the price 16.6% above a 200-day average that has just turned up), but not into B because guidance was only repeated, the upgrades are cost-led with sales revisions flat to negative, and about three-quarters of the price gain is sector-wide with Pernod Ricard, the closest peer, weakest of all.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity: a simple, bounded earnings case with political tails and a wide price range

Conclusion: Diageo's earnings case is simple and bounded, with an EPS range of about ±5-6%, but its tails are negative and political, and the range of share-price outcomes is several times wider than the range of earnings outcomes.

Simplicity. The earnings case fits in one sentence: keep about 40% of the $910m of savings due by FY2028, and repay about $5bn of debt. Both drivers are internal, dated and visible in advance, which makes the earnings case simple. Two things are not simple: the franchise outcome cannot be traced through anything the company discloses, and the share price depends on something else again, the sector multiple.

The five judgements, with the arithmetic. The base for the sums is FY2028 EPS of $1.77 on 2,221m shares and a 24% tax rate, so $100m of operating profit equals $76m of net income, 3.4c of EPS, or 1.9% of EPS.

JudgementBaseIf wrong by a plausible amountWorkingEffect on EPS

2. Savings kept after reinvestment40% of $910m = $364m by FY202830% (Jefferies' figure) or 50% (the company's)10 points x $910m = $91m of operating profit (49 basis points of margin); x 0.76 = $69m; ÷ 2,221m±3.1c (±1.8%)
Gross margin (60) basis points in FY2027Morgan Stanley's (239)179 basis points x $19,034m = $341m; x 0.76 = $259m; ÷ 2,225m(11.6)c (7)% before any offset from spending less elsewhere

Three conclusions follow from the table.

Judgement 1, the multiple, dwarfs the rest. The plausible range of FY2028 EPS is about $1.65 to $1.87, roughly ±6%. The multiple's plausible range moves the share price by (19)% to +58%.
Judgements 2 and 3 offset each other in EPS and compound in franchise quality. Management controls lever 2, the savings kept, and can use it to absorb a miss on lever 3, North American sales. That offset narrows the range of EPS and widens the range of franchise health, which is why a composition miss (point 4 of the summary) is the disappointment to expect.
Judgement 5, US trade policy, is where the true tails are. Its sub-cases differ greatly in size, so I separate them below.

Trade policy, updated: the AlphaSense research resolves one worry, raises another and leaves the largest in place.

Resolved

Canadian whisky is better protected than the headlines suggest. The US measure on Canadian alcohol (a 50% tariff from August 2026, then an import ban on packaged product from late September) excludes bulk spirits in containers above four litres. Diageo closed its Ontario bottling plant in February 2026 and bottles Crown Royal for the US inside the US. The residual risks are the bulk exemption being closed and a Canadian consumer boycott.

Raised

The EU tariff assumption in guidance is already out of date. Guidance assumes a 10% tariff on EU imports (Guinness, Baileys). On 25 November the US Trade Representative proposed 15%, rising to 20% if talks fail, with hearings from 25 January 2027. I cannot split the $100m gross tariff cost between its parts. If half is European, each five points of EU tariff costs about $25m gross and under 1c of EPS: an irritant, not a thesis risk.

Still in place

Tequila is the exposure that matters. Don Julio and Casamigos make up 24% of US sales and cannot be made outside Mexico. On 1 July 2026 the US declined to extend the North American trade agreement, which now faces annual review; the next comment deadline is 12 January 2027.

Tails and precedents.

  • Probability. I put the chance of events outside the EPS range at 10-12% over 18 months. Almost all such events are negative, and they are either political or in the distribution channel (one large US distributor entered liquidation in July 2026).
  • How Diageo's shocks have arrived. Diageo's shocks have always arrived through revenue, and through channel inventory that management could not see: the FY2015 destock, and the November 2023 Latin American warning (shares (11)% in a day, consensus EPS (17)% in twelve months). Diageo's past downgrade cycles lasted 9-24 months and cut EPS by 20-27%. The current cycle has run 36 months and cut EPS by 18%, so it is late, and it has already lasted longer than any before it.
  • Suddenness. Monthly US retail data move the shares while predicting reported sales only loosely. Trade measures arrive by decree.
  • Downside to a trough multiple. A multiple of 11 times on unchanged earnings implies a share price about 19% lower; with earnings 10% lower, about 27% lower. Morgan Stanley's bear cases are 37-40% below today's price.

Strongest counter-case, both ways. Risk may be lower than it looks: estimates are rebased, charges taken, the dividend reset and the multiple at the bottom of its history. Risk may be higher than it looks: leverage of 3.1 times makes Diageo a leveraged defensive, and the 45% rally from the low was mostly the sector's.

What would change my view. Completion of both disposals would remove the main balance-sheet timing risk; the EABL sale still faces court challenges in Kenya, and the cricket-team sale awaits the cricket board's approval before a long-stop date in mid-December. A matched price war or a tariff on Mexican imports would move the case from "bounded" to "open".

Against the market. Broker research airs the risks well, with three exceptions: the clash between the buyback story and the company's own leverage target, the mixed basis of published consensus, and the gap between the tariff guidance and the latest US proposal.

Score: 53, set by the Rater. The earnings case is simple and narrow (FY2027 EPS 75% likely within 3% of $1.68, FY2028 cone about ±6%, resting on two dated internal drivers: savings and debt repayment), but leverage is 3.1 times (78th percentile), the franchise cannot be tracked through disclosure, Diageo's shocks have historically come suddenly through channel inventory ((11)% in a day in 2023), the tails are political and negative (a Mexican tariff costs up to 11.6% of EPS) and the share price swings (19)% to +58% on a sector-set multiple. That is above the groups' average of 48 for the narrow cone, between NKT's visible but execution-exposed case and IMCD's leveraged, downgrade-prone one.

#10 Lifecycle: bottomed and turning up, on the threshold of broadening

Conclusion: Diageo's shares are turning up, at the threshold of thesis broadening, and the test of that step falls between February and August 2027.

Evidence.

Bottomed. The multiple touched 10.9 times in March 2026. Since then guidance has been rebased, about $2.3bn of impairments and restructuring has been charged, the dividend has been halved and the chief executive replaced. Estimates fell 14-15% from their peak, and revisions have turned.
→
Turning up. The shares are 45% above their low and above a 200-day average that has only just begun to rise. Buy ratings are climbing from a cautious base.
→
Not yet broadening. The thesis has one leg, cost and cash. Sales estimates are still drifting down, and no upgrade engine is running. Company-specific factors explain under a quarter of the six-month share-price gain. Short interest of 0.4% means there are no forced buyers left to help.

Inference. The dashboard's rule places Diageo in the Broadening phase. I place it half a step earlier: turning up, on the threshold of broadening. A thesis broadens when new kinds of evidence recruit new kinds of buyer. For Diageo, the new evidence would be the first buyback and the first sign of US share holding, and neither has happened.

So what. The half-step matters for the fair multiple (#11), because the fair multiple sits lower in the range while forecasts are still being proven. The half-step also sets expectations for the path of the shares. The evidence arrives in reverse order of importance: cost in February 2027, cash and capital returns in August 2027, and market share in FY2028. For about nine months, the sector and the monthly US data will set the share price more than anything Diageo reports.

Strongest counter-case. Price may lead fundamentals. The market may already be recognising a broadening that fundamentals will confirm later, as it did after the FY2015 destock, when the shares re-rated before growth returned. Alternatively, the turn may stall: under Lewis, Tesco's profit recovered within 18 months, yet its shares went nowhere for his whole tenure.

What would change my view. Towards broadening: a buyback announced, EPS revisions positive on a clean basis, and Diageo's US share loss narrowing in the monthly data. Towards stalling: a result that meets on EPS and misses on composition, followed by estimate cuts for FY2028.

Against the market. Broker ratings (a mean of Overweight) imply that the market accepts the turn. I agree that the stock is turning, and I think the turn is earlier than the share price suggests.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. Bottomed and turning: the multiple troughed at 10.9 times, guidance, charges and the dividend are rebased, revisions have turned after a 36-month downgrade cycle and the price is above a just-rising 200-day average, so the computed Turning/Inflecting is right; but the thesis has one leg (cost and cash), sales estimates still drift down, no guidance raise has come and the gain is mostly the sector's, so I agree with the memo that it is short of Broadening. It sits just below Kerry's mid-cycle Reinforcing and above Nexans' paused Reinforcing.

#11 The fair multiple: 16 to 17.5 times over 18 months, with 21.6 times as the bull case

Conclusion: the guideline's 21.6 times describes what Diageo's shares are worth if the old growth algorithm returns; on today's evidence I judge 16 to 17.5 times fair over 18 months.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline gives a fair multiple of 21.6 times two-year forward earnings: the 80th percentile of the stock's ten-year history, the level the guideline assigns to a stock in the Broadening phase. That guideline multiple is 56% above today's 13.8 times.

My view: 21.6 times is the right destination for the bull case and too high as the 18-month centre. I would centre on 16 to 17.5 times.

Five reasons for centring below the guideline.

  1. Phase. I judge the stock to be half a step earlier than Broadening (#10).
  2. The valuation history describes a different business. The stock last traded at 21.6 times in April 2022. Every one of its 23 months at or above that level fell in 2019 or in 2020-22, when Diageo was growing sales at 5% or more, lifting EPS by about 10% a year and buying back shares. The stock has not traded above 16.7 times in the last two years. Its median since mid-2023 is 15.5 times, and its median over the last five years is 16.5 times.
  3. The valuation history also reflects a different discount rate. A rough rule says that a fair multiple equals cash conversion divided by the cost of equity minus long-run growth. With 85% conversion and an 8% cost of equity, growth of 2.5% (the company's own FY2029 target) supports 15.5 times, growth of 3% supports 17 times, and growth of 4% (Diageo's 40-year average) supports 21 times. So 21.6 times is the multiple of the old belief in 4% growth. The same 2.5% growth at a 7% cost of equity gives 18.9 times, which equals the ten-year median: much of that median was earned when bond yields were far lower.
  4. Diageo's multiple is mostly not Diageo's to set. About two-thirds of the multiple's movement follows the spirits industry. Every listed alcohol company trades at or near the bottom tenth of its own range, except Rémy Cointreau and AB InBev at about the bottom third. A move to the 80th percentile therefore needs the industry to re-rate, and an industry re-rating needs US spirits volumes to stop falling.
  5. Precedents for cost-led recoveries point the same way. Multiples returned to their medians only once volume growth was positive. Pernod Ricard reached 21 times after 2018 and Carlsberg 23 times by 2019, both with sales growing and the sector on about 20 times. Heineken has delivered its savings and sits at 13.5 times. AB InBev is at 15 times after four years of delivery.

Strongest counter-case, for the guideline. A 2nd-percentile reading on a franchise of Diageo's quality is itself extreme, and reversion from extremes is usually faster than fundamentals. At the low of the FY2015 destock Diageo still traded on 19 times, because the market trusted growth to return, and growth did return. European beverage stocks trade at an 11% discount to the market, against a 50% premium in 2019. If rates ease and the US turns, 21.6 times will look ordinary.

How I weight the multiple at December 2027. 21.6 times or more: 10%. 16 to 18 times: 40%. Unchanged at 13 to 15 times: 35%. 12 times or below: 15%. Those weights centre near 15.6 times. By mid-2029, with the plan delivered and buybacks running, I would centre at 17-18 times and give 21.6 times a 25-30% chance.

What would change my view. Towards the guideline: US share holding before FY2028, organic growth guided at 3% or more, or a fall in bond yields. Away from the guideline: a second year of flat organic sales.

Against the market. The average broker target implies about 15-15.5 times. Jefferies argues for more than 20 times on execution; Deutsche Bank says 14 times "appropriately reflects a lower growth outlook". I am a little above the broker average and well below both the guideline and Jefferies.

Score: 79, set by the Rater. Cheap on its own range and neutral against peers gives B; I place it in the lower part of the band because much of the cheapness is deserved, since the ten-year history was set when Diageo grew sales 5% and EPS 10% a year at lower bond yields, the stock is turning rather than broadening, and the whole alcohol sector is near the bottom of its ranges, but above the floor because the own-range reading is as extreme as it gets and the peer reading leans cheap.

#12 Total shareholder return: about +19% probability-weighted, on a dependable 7% a year

Conclusion: the model's +73% is almost entirely the guideline multiple; the dependable return is about 7% a year from earnings and dividends, and my probability-weighted return to December 2027 is about +19%, with the skew to the upside.

The return of record. At the guideline multiple, the model gives:

HorizonTotal returnAnnualisedFrom the multipleFrom earningsFrom dividends
To 31 December 2027+73.0%+64.7%+56.2%+9.5%+2.0%
To 30 June 2029+95.2%+29.4%+56.2%+20.9%+6.4%

The multiple and earnings components multiply, and dividends add. The model's value per share is £33.46 at December 2027 and £37.75 at June 2029, against a starting price of £19.34.

What drives each component.

  • The multiple (+56.2%). This component is the move from 13.8 to 21.6 times and nothing else. It supplies about three-quarters of the 18-month return and three-fifths of the three-year return. It is the guideline's assumption, not an output of the forecasts.
  • Earnings (+9.5% and +20.9%). This component compares two-year forward EPS today with the same measure at each horizon. It rolls the earnings window from FY2028-29 out to FY2029-30 and then to FY2031, so it captures the full savings, finance charges about $180m lower than in FY2026, and buybacks of $1.5bn rising to $2bn a year. One caution: the model's EPS is before minorities, and today's consensus is after them. Like for like, the earnings component is about +5% and +14%, so the return of record is overstated by about seven points at 18 months and eleven points at three years.
  • Dividends (+2.0% and +6.4%). A 51c dividend grows 6-7% a year on a payout of about 31%. Buybacks reach shareholders through EPS, not through the dividend line.

The same arithmetic at other multiples (EPS on the brokers' basis; my arithmetic).

Inference: three points.

~7% a yearThe floor return is earnings plus dividends, about 7% a year, and it is the high-confidence part of the return.
+19%The distribution of returns is skewed to the upside. On the weights in #11, the probability-weighted return to December 2027 is about +19%. The upside cases (50% combined) average about +37%, and the downside case (15%) loses about 16%.
~(3)% at 11xTime helps. By mid-2029 even the trough multiple roughly returns the money invested, because earnings and dividends have had time to accumulate.

Strongest counter-case. Any single multiple overstates precision in either direction. If the guideline is right, I am understating the return by about 45 points. If Deutsche Bank's reading of the sector is right, the 35% weight I give to an unchanged multiple is too low, and the return is the 7% floor.

What would change my view. The same evidence as for the fair multiple (#11). Each turn of the multiple is worth about 7% of the share price, far more than any plausible revision to earnings.

Against the market. The average broker target implies a return of about 9-13%, plus a 2% yield, over twelve months. My estimate is above the broker average and far below the return of record.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. About +19% gives C, just under the B line, and maps to about 72; the three-year check is supportive (about +45% at the five-year median multiple, and even the trough multiple about returns the money by mid-2029) and the skew is to the upside (50% weight averaging +37% against 15% losing about 16%), but the return rests on a sector-led re-rating with a dependable part of only about 7% a year, so I hold it at the top of C rather than lifting it.

#13 Summary conclusion: a credible floor now, and a case worth watching for US share

Diageo offers a high-quality franchise with a credible earnings floor, at a trough multiple, at the end of a long downgrade cycle. The earnings floor is real because it rests on cost removal and debt repayment, which management controls, has dated and has recently over-delivered. That floor makes a loss from earnings unlikely over the next 18 months and puts about 7% a year under the shares before any re-rating.

Diageo does not yet offer what Richard looks for most: outcomes and upgrade probabilities unusually skewed to the positive. Earnings forecasts are on consensus, profit guidance has no cushion, and the plausible surprises in cash and buybacks are small. The return beyond the floor depends on a re-rating, and two-thirds of any re-rating belongs to an industry whose largest market is still shrinking.

The constructive way to hold these two facts together is as a sequence of three stages. The first stage, now, is "downgrades stop": well evidenced and partly priced. The second stage, in 2027, is "cash comes back": dated, mostly in management's hands, and likely to be smaller than the optimists expect. The third stage is "share holds in the US": the only stage that changes the multiple band, the least proven, and the stage where early evidence would be worth most. The case deserves close attention for that third stage, and the monthly US data are where it will show first.

The four memo ratings.

53 Thesis's Change Forces' Strength, set by the Rater. Strong, funded internal change (68) is largely cancelled by a moderate external headwind (35), so the net force is only mildly positive; it reaches profits surely because savings and debt repayment are in management's hands, but only as EPS growth of about 4.5-5.5% a year (D 46), well below the Universe median, with no step-up in earnings power, so it sits just above neutral.
64 Foundations' Robustness, set by the Rater. Quality of the business (62) rests on a global, time- and regulation-protected franchise with top-quintile margins, which makes the foundations sturdier than typical; it is held in the 60s because US pricing power is negative and share is slipping, leverage is 3.1 times, returns on recent capital are poor, and the delivery record (44) has one good year after a warning, an abandoned target and a cut.
58 Setups' Fit/Crispness, set by the Rater. The case fits 'cause for concern clearing in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business on a first-quartile multiple' in kind (two concerns, the balance sheet and downgrades, are clearing), but its largest concern, US share and pricing, is a current problem in the business that is not yet clearing, which blurs the mechanism the setup needs.
57 Case Riskiness, set by the Rater. Over Riskiness and simplicity (53): the earnings risks are close to Richard's 'paper cuts' (a ±5-6% cone on dated, controllable drivers) and the multiple sits at the bottom of its range, which caps a trough fall at about 19%; but 3.1 times leverage, political tails on tequila, a profit guide with no cushion and a share price set by a sector multiple keep it well short of the CVS-style 80s.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
